captions.instagram:
How does a torch work?

Two cells, a spring, a switch and a mirror shaped like a parabola. Take a torch apart in 3D, follow the current round its loop, and trace the rays that turn a tiny lamp into a beam.

→ A torch is two cells, a spring, a switch, a lamp and a mirror in a tube.
→ The tail spring is not just a spring: it is a wire that carries the current.
→ Current needs a closed loop: cell, lamp, strip, switch, strip, spring, and back into the cell.
→ As cells run down they push less and waste more inside, so the bulb fades to orange.
→ A filament bulb turns about 3% of its energy into light; a white LED manages about 40%.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/torchclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a torch work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Two cells, a spring, a switch and a mirror shaped like a parabola. Take a torch apart in 3D, follow the current round its loop, and trace the rays that turn a tiny lamp into a beam.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/torchclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/torchclear

In this video:
• Ten parts in a tube. A torch is two cells, a spring, two metal strips, a switch, a lamp, a reflector, a lens and a case.
• One closed loop. Current flows only round a complete circuit: out of the cell's + cap, through the lamp, along a strip to the switch, along another strip to the spring and back into the − end.
• A hot wire against a glowing chip. A filament bulb makes light by being white-hot, at about 2,450 K, and wastes nearly all its energy as heat: about 8 lumens per watt.
• A parabola makes the beam. The reflector is a parabola.
• What is inside the cells. In a zinc-carbon cell the can itself is the fuel, which is why flat ones leak.
• Torches with no shop-bought cells. A shake torch slides a magnet through a coil: the changing field makes a voltage, a capacitor stores the charge and an LED uses it.
